Artificial Neuron¶

Components of Neural Networks¶

Overview¶

The artificial neuron is the fundamental building block of neural networks. This component mimics the basic operation of biological neurons by computing a weighted sum of inputs, adding a bias term, and applying an activation function.

Definition¶

A single artificial neuron implements the mathematical function:

$$ y = f(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b) $$

Where:

  • $\mathbf{x}$ is the input vector
  • $\mathbf{w}$ is the weight vector
  • $b$ is the bias term
  • $f$ is the activation function
  • $y$ is the output

This component forms the basis for all neural network architectures.

Mathematical Formulation¶

Components¶

Symbol Name Description
$\mathbf{x}$ Input vector $[x_1, x_2, ..., x_n]$
$\mathbf{w}$ Weight vector $[w_1, w_2, ..., w_n]$
$b$ Bias Scalar offset
$z$ Pre-activation $\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b$
$f$ Activation function Non-linear transformation
Output $y$ Scalar output

Computation Steps¶

  1. Linear combination: $z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b$
  2. Activation: $y = f(z)$

Common Activation Functions¶

The choice of activation function $f$ is crucial for the neuron's behavior. Here are some commonly used functions:

  • Sigmoid: $f(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$
  • ReLU: $f(z) = \max(0, z)$
  • Tanh: $f(z) = \tanh(z)$

For a comprehensive study of activation functions, their properties, and implementations, see the Activation Functions notebook.

The following diagrams illustrate the structure and data flow of a single neuron:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches
import numpy as np

def draw_single_neuron():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 10))  # Increased height
    
    # Define positions
    input_x = -4
    input_ys = [3, 2, 1, -1]  # Skip 0 for dots
    bias_pos = (-2, 4)
    neuron_pos = (0, 1.5)
    output_pos = (4, 1.5)
    activation_pos = (2, 1.5)
    
    # Draw input nodes
    input_labels = ['$x_1$', '$x_2$', '$x_3$', '$x_n$']
    for i, (y, label) in enumerate(zip(input_ys, input_labels)):
        circle = patches.Circle((input_x, y), 0.3, facecolor='lightgreen', 
                               edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
        ax.add_patch(circle)
        ax.text(input_x, y, label, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw dots
    ax.text(input_x, 0, '⋮', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=20)
    
    # Draw bias node
    bias_circle = patches.Circle(bias_pos, 0.3, facecolor='yellow', 
                                edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.add_patch(bias_circle)
    ax.text(bias_pos[0], bias_pos[1], '$b$', ha='center', va='center', 
            fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw neuron (summation)
    neuron_circle = patches.Circle(neuron_pos, 0.5, facecolor='lightblue', 
                                  edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.add_patch(neuron_circle)
    ax.text(neuron_pos[0], neuron_pos[1], '$\\Sigma$', ha='center', va='center', 
            fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw activation function
    ax.text(activation_pos[0], activation_pos[1], '$f$', ha='center', va='center', 
            fontsize=14, fontweight='bold', 
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor='white', edgecolor='black'))
    
    # Draw output node
    output_circle = patches.Circle(output_pos, 0.3, facecolor='lightcoral', 
                                  edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
    ax.add_patch(output_circle)
    ax.text(output_pos[0], output_pos[1], '$y$', ha='center', va='center', 
            fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw arrows from inputs to neuron
    weight_labels = ['$w_1$', '$w_2$', '$w_3$', '$w_n$']
    for i, (y, w_label) in enumerate(zip(input_ys, weight_labels)):
        # Arrow
        ax.annotate('', xy=(neuron_pos[0]-0.5, neuron_pos[1]), 
                   xytext=(input_x+0.3, y),
                   arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))
        # Weight label
        mid_x = (input_x + neuron_pos[0]) / 2
        mid_y = (y + neuron_pos[1]) / 2
        offset_y = 0.2 if y > neuron_pos[1] else -0.2
        ax.text(mid_x, mid_y + offset_y, w_label, ha='center', va='center', 
                fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw arrow from bias to neuron
    ax.annotate('', xy=(neuron_pos[0]-0.3, neuron_pos[1]+0.3), 
               xytext=(bias_pos[0]+0.2, bias_pos[1]-0.2),
               arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))
    ax.text((bias_pos[0] + neuron_pos[0])/2 - 0.3, (bias_pos[1] + neuron_pos[1])/2, 
            '1', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Draw arrow from neuron to activation
    ax.annotate('', xy=(activation_pos[0]-0.3, activation_pos[1]), 
               xytext=(neuron_pos[0]+0.5, neuron_pos[1]),
               arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))
    
    # Draw arrow from activation to output
    ax.annotate('', xy=(output_pos[0]-0.3, output_pos[1]), 
               xytext=(activation_pos[0]+0.3, activation_pos[1]),
               arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))
    
    # Add mathematical expression at the bottom (moved higher to avoid cutting)
    ax.text(0, -1.2, r'$y = f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b\right)$', 
            ha='center', va='center', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.5", facecolor='lightyellow', alpha=0.8))
    
    # Set axis properties with more margin at bottom
    ax.set_xlim(-5, 5)
    ax.set_ylim(-2, 5)  # Extended bottom margin
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title('Single Neuron Architecture', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', pad=20)
    
    # Use subplots_adjust to ensure everything fits
    plt.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.1, top=0.9)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

This diagram shows:

  • Input nodes ($x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots, x_n$): The input features
  • Weights ($w_1, w_2, w_3, \ldots, w_n$): Parameters that scale each input
  • Bias ($b$): Additional parameter added to the weighted sum
  • Summation ($\sum$): The neuron computes the weighted sum of inputs plus bias
  • Activation function ($f$): Applies non-linearity to the sum
  • Output ($y$): The final result of the neuron

PyTorch Implementation¶

Here's a simple implementation of the single neuron component using PyTorch:

In [18]:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SingleNeuron(nn.Module):
    """
    Implementation of a single artificial neuron.
    
    Computes: y = f(w^T * x + b)
    where f is the activation function (sigmoid in this case)
    """
    
    def __init__(self, input_dim):
        """
        Args:
            input_dim (int): Number of input features
        """
        super(SingleNeuron, self).__init__()
        # Linear layer: performs w^T * x + b
        self.linear = nn.Linear(input_dim, 1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward pass through the neuron.
        
        Args:
            x (torch.Tensor): Input tensor of shape (batch_size, input_dim)
            
        Returns:
            torch.Tensor: Output tensor of shape (batch_size, 1)
        """
        # Step 1: Linear transformation (weighted sum + bias)
        z = self.linear(x)
        
        # Step 2: Apply activation function (sigmoid)
        y = torch.sigmoid(z)
        
        return y

# Example usage
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print("=== Single Neuron Component Demo ===")
    
    # Set random seed for reproducibility
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    
    # Create a neuron with 3 input features
    neuron = SingleNeuron(input_dim=3)
    
    # Display the neuron's parameters
    print(f"Weights: {neuron.linear.weight.data}")
    print(f"Bias: {neuron.linear.bias.data}")
    
    # Create sample input data (batch of 5 samples)
    X = torch.randn(5, 3)
    print(f"\nInput shape: {X.shape}")
    print(f"Input data:\n{X}")
    
    # Forward pass through the neuron
    outputs = neuron(X)
    print(f"\nOutput shape: {outputs.shape}")
    print(f"Outputs:\n{outputs}")
    
    # Show the computation step by step for the first sample
    print(f"\n=== Step-by-step computation for first sample ===")
    x_sample = X[0]  # First sample
    w = neuron.linear.weight.data.squeeze()  # Weights
    b = neuron.linear.bias.data.item()       # Bias
    
    # Manual computation
    z_manual = torch.dot(w, x_sample) + b
    y_manual = torch.sigmoid(z_manual)
    
    print(f"Input: {x_sample}")
    print(f"Weights: {w}")
    print(f"Bias: {b:.4f}")
    print(f"Linear combination (z): {z_manual:.4f}")
    print(f"After activation (y): {y_manual:.4f}")
    print(f"Network output: {outputs[0].item():.4f}")
    print(f"Match: {abs(y_manual - outputs[0].item()) < 1e-6}")

Decision Boundary and Classification in 2D¶

Mathematical Foundation¶

A single neuron can perform binary classification by learning a decision boundary that separates two classes in the input space. This is the core concept that generalizes to hyperplanes in higher dimensions.

Decision Boundary Equation¶

For a 2D input $\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2]^T$, the neuron computes:

$$z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b$$

The decision boundary is defined by the set of points where $z = 0$:

$$w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b = 0$$

This can be rearranged to the line equation:

$$x_2 = -\frac{w_1}{w_2} x_1 - \frac{b}{w_2}$$

Classification Rule¶

With sigmoid activation $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$:

  • Class 1 (positive): $z > 0 \Rightarrow \sigma(z) > 0.5$
  • Class 0 (negative): $z < 0 \Rightarrow \sigma(z) < 0.5$
  • Decision boundary: $z = 0 \Rightarrow \sigma(z) = 0.5$

Geometric Interpretation¶

  • Weight vector $\mathbf{w} = [w_1, w_2]^T$ is perpendicular to the decision boundary
  • Bias $b$ controls the distance of the line from the origin
  • The neuron classifies points based on which side of the line they fall on

Important Mathematical Clarifications¶

Before diving into decision boundaries, let's clarify the key mathematical distinctions:

Notation Convention¶

Symbol Name Description Example
$z$ Pre-activation Linear combination: $z = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b$ $z = 2.5$
$y$ Output After activation: $y = f(z)$ $y = \sigma(2.5) = 0.924$
$t$ Target/Label True value or class label $t = 1$ (class) or $t = 3.7$ (regression)

Two Main Tasks¶

Classification Task:

  • Activation: Sigmoid $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$
  • Decision rule: $z > 0 \Rightarrow$ Class 1, $z < 0 \Rightarrow$ Class 0
  • Decision boundary: $z = 0$ (equivalently $y = 0.5$)
  • Loss function: Binary Cross-Entropy $L = -[t \log y + (1-t) \log(1-y)]$

Regression Task:

  • Activation: Linear $f(z) = z$ (no activation)
  • Prediction: $y = z = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b$
  • Loss function: Mean Square Error $L = \frac{1}{2}(y - t)^2$

Why This Matters¶

The decision boundary is fundamentally about the pre-activation $z$:

  • Geometric boundary: $z = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b = 0$
  • Classification threshold: When $z = 0$, then $\sigma(z) = 0.5$
  • Weight vector interpretation: $\mathbf{w}$ is perpendicular to the boundary $z = 0$
In [24]:
# Mathematical demonstration: z vs y, MSE vs BCE
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Create sample data
torch.manual_seed(42)
x = torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])  # Input
t_regression = torch.tensor([[2.1], [3.9], [6.2], [7.8]])  # Regression targets
t_classification = torch.tensor([[0.0], [0.0], [1.0], [1.0]])  # Classification targets

# Single neuron with different activations
class RegressionNeuron(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(1, 1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.linear(x)  # No activation for regression
        return z

class ClassificationNeuron(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(1, 1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.linear(x)
        y = torch.sigmoid(z)  # Sigmoid activation for classification
        return z, y  # Return both z and y for clarity

# Initialize neurons
reg_neuron = RegressionNeuron()
cls_neuron = ClassificationNeuron()

# Set some example weights for demonstration
with torch.no_grad():
    reg_neuron.linear.weight.fill_(1.8)
    reg_neuron.linear.bias.fill_(0.5)
    cls_neuron.linear.weight.fill_(2.0)
    cls_neuron.linear.bias.fill_(-5.0)

print("=== Mathematical Notation Demonstration ===\n")

# Regression example
print("📊 REGRESSION TASK:")
y_reg = reg_neuron(x)
mse_loss = nn.MSELoss()(y_reg, t_regression)
print(f"Input x: {x.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"Linear output y = z: {y_reg.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"Target t: {t_regression.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"MSE Loss: {mse_loss.item():.4f}")
print(f"Formula: L = (1/2)*(y - t)²\n")

# Classification example  
print("🎯 CLASSIFICATION TASK:")
z_cls, y_cls = cls_neuron(x)
bce_loss = nn.BCELoss()(y_cls, t_classification)
print(f"Input x: {x.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"Pre-activation z: {z_cls.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"Output y = σ(z): {y_cls.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"Target t: {t_classification.squeeze().tolist()}")
print(f"BCE Loss: {bce_loss.item():.4f}")
print(f"Formula: L = -[t*log(y) + (1-t)*log(1-y)]")

# Decision boundary analysis
print(f"\n🔍 DECISION BOUNDARY ANALYSIS:")
print(f"Decision boundary occurs when z = 0")
print(f"Current weight: {cls_neuron.linear.weight.item():.2f}")
print(f"Current bias: {cls_neuron.linear.bias.item():.2f}")
print(f"Boundary equation: {cls_neuron.linear.weight.item():.2f}*x + {cls_neuron.linear.bias.item():.2f} = 0")
boundary_x = -cls_neuron.linear.bias.item() / cls_neuron.linear.weight.item()
print(f"Boundary at x = {boundary_x:.2f}")
print(f"At boundary: z = 0, y = σ(0) = 0.5")

# Visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

# Plot 1: Regression
ax1 = axes[0]
x_plot = np.linspace(0.5, 4.5, 100)
y_plot_reg = reg_neuron.linear.weight.item() * x_plot + reg_neuron.linear.bias.item()

ax1.scatter(x.numpy(), t_regression.numpy(), color='red', s=80, label='Target t', zorder=5)
ax1.scatter(x.numpy(), y_reg.detach().numpy(), color='blue', s=80, label='Prediction y', zorder=5)
ax1.plot(x_plot, y_plot_reg, 'blue', linewidth=2, label='y = wx + b')
ax1.set_xlabel('Input x')
ax1.set_ylabel('Output')
ax1.set_title('Regression: y = z = wx + b\n(Linear activation)')
ax1.legend()
ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Plot 2: Classification - z values
ax2 = axes[1]  
z_plot = cls_neuron.linear.weight.item() * x_plot + cls_neuron.linear.bias.item()
ax2.scatter(x.numpy(), z_cls.detach().numpy(), color='green', s=80, label='Pre-activation z', zorder=5)
ax2.plot(x_plot, z_plot, 'green', linewidth=2, label='z = wx + b')
ax2.axhline(y=0, color='black', linestyle='--', label='Decision boundary (z=0)')
ax2.axvline(x=boundary_x, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, label=f'x = {boundary_x:.2f}')
ax2.set_xlabel('Input x')
ax2.set_ylabel('Pre-activation z')
ax2.set_title('Classification: Pre-activation z\n(Before sigmoid)')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Plot 3: Classification - y values
ax3 = axes[2]
y_plot_cls = torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(z_plot)).numpy()
ax3.scatter(x.numpy(), t_classification.numpy(), color='red', s=80, label='Target t', zorder=5)
ax3.scatter(x.numpy(), y_cls.detach().numpy(), color='blue', s=80, label='Prediction y', zorder=5)
ax3.plot(x_plot, y_plot_cls, 'blue', linewidth=2, label='y = σ(z)')
ax3.axhline(y=0.5, color='black', linestyle='--', label='Decision threshold (y=0.5)')
ax3.axvline(x=boundary_x, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, label=f'x = {boundary_x:.2f}')
ax3.set_xlabel('Input x')
ax3.set_ylabel('Output y')
ax3.set_title('Classification: Output y = σ(z)\n(After sigmoid)')
ax3.legend()
ax3.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"\n📚 KEY TAKEAWAYS:")
print(f"1. z is the LINEAR combination (pre-activation)")
print(f"2. y is the OUTPUT after activation function")
print(f"3. Decision boundary is where z = 0 (equivalently y = 0.5 for sigmoid)")
print(f"4. MSE for regression, BCE for classification")
print(f"5. The geometric boundary equation uses z, not y")

Visual Representation of Decision Boundary¶

The following diagrams illustrate how a single neuron creates a linear decision boundary in 2D space:

In [19]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.patches as patches

def draw_decision_boundary_concept():
    """
    Draw a conceptual diagram showing decision boundary, weight vector, and classification regions.
    """
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6))
    
    # === Left plot: Decision Boundary Concept ===
    ax1.set_title('Decision Boundary Concept', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Define example parameters
    w1, w2, b = 1.5, 1.0, -0.5
    
    # Create decision boundary line
    x1_range = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
    x2_line = -(w1/w2) * x1_range - (b/w2)  # x2 = -(w1/w2)*x1 - (b/w2)
    
    # Plot decision boundary
    ax1.plot(x1_range, x2_line, 'k-', linewidth=3, label=f'Decision Boundary\n{w1:.1f}x₁ + {w2:.1f}x₂ + {b:.1f} = 0')
    
    # Add colored regions
    x1_mesh, x2_mesh = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 50), np.linspace(-3, 3, 50))
    z_mesh = w1 * x1_mesh + w2 * x2_mesh + b
    
    # Color regions
    ax1.contourf(x1_mesh, x2_mesh, z_mesh, levels=[z_mesh.min(), 0, z_mesh.max()], 
                colors=['lightcoral', 'lightblue'], alpha=0.3)
    ax1.contour(x1_mesh, x2_mesh, z_mesh, levels=[0], colors=['black'], linewidths=3)
    
    # Add weight vector (perpendicular to boundary)
    # Weight vector starts from origin
    weight_scale = 1.5
    ax1.arrow(0, 0, w1*weight_scale, w2*weight_scale, head_width=0.1, head_length=0.1, 
             fc='red', ec='red', linewidth=2, label=f'Weight Vector\nw = [{w1:.1f}, {w2:.1f}]')
    
    # Add sample points
    # Class 0 points (negative side)
    class0_x1 = [-2.5, -1.8, -2.0]
    class0_x2 = [2.0, 1.5, 2.5]
    ax1.scatter(class0_x1, class0_x2, c='red', s=80, marker='o', edgecolors='darkred', 
               linewidth=2, label='Class 0 (z < 0)', zorder=5)
    
    # Class 1 points (positive side)
    class1_x1 = [2.0, 1.5, 2.5]
    class1_x2 = [-1.5, -2.0, -1.0]
    ax1.scatter(class1_x1, class1_x2, c='blue', s=80, marker='s', edgecolors='darkblue', 
               linewidth=2, label='Class 1 (z > 0)', zorder=5)
    
    # Add perpendicular line to show weight vector relationship
    # Find a point on the decision boundary
    x1_perp = 0.5
    x2_perp = -(w1/w2) * x1_perp - (b/w2)
    
    # Draw perpendicular line from boundary point
    perp_length = 0.8
    normal_x = w1 / np.sqrt(w1**2 + w2**2)
    normal_y = w2 / np.sqrt(w1**2 + w2**2)
    
    ax1.plot([x1_perp - perp_length*normal_x, x1_perp + perp_length*normal_x],
             [x2_perp - perp_length*normal_y, x2_perp + perp_length*normal_y],
             'r--', linewidth=2, alpha=0.7)
    
    # Add annotations
    ax1.text(-2, -2, 'Class 0 Region\n(z < 0, σ(z) < 0.5)', fontsize=10, 
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor='lightcoral', alpha=0.7))
    ax1.text(2, 2, 'Class 1 Region\n(z > 0, σ(z) > 0.5)', fontsize=10,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor='lightblue', alpha=0.7))
    
    ax1.set_xlim(-3, 3)
    ax1.set_ylim(-3, 3)
    ax1.set_xlabel('x₁', fontsize=12)
    ax1.set_ylabel('x₂', fontsize=12)
    ax1.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax1.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
    ax1.set_aspect('equal')
    
    # === Right plot: Effect of Parameters ===
    ax2.set_title('Effect of Parameters on Decision Boundary', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    
    # Show multiple decision boundaries with different parameters
    x1_range = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
    
    # Different weight combinations
    params = [
        (1.0, 1.0, 0, 'w=[1,1], b=0', 'blue'),
        (2.0, 0.5, 0, 'w=[2,0.5], b=0', 'red'),
        (1.0, 1.0, 1, 'w=[1,1], b=1', 'green'),
        (1.0, 1.0, -1, 'w=[1,1], b=-1', 'orange')
    ]
    
    for w1, w2, b, label, color in params:
        x2_line = -(w1/w2) * x1_range - (b/w2)
        ax2.plot(x1_range, x2_line, color=color, linewidth=2, label=label)
        
        # Add weight vector for each
        scale = 1.0
        ax2.arrow(0, 0, w1*scale, w2*scale, head_width=0.08, head_length=0.08,
                 fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.7, linewidth=1.5)
    
    # Add origin point
    ax2.plot(0, 0, 'ko', markersize=8, label='Origin')
    
    ax2.set_xlim(-3, 3)
    ax2.set_ylim(-3, 3)
    ax2.set_xlabel('x₁', fontsize=12)
    ax2.set_ylabel('x₂', fontsize=12)
    ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax2.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9)
    ax2.set_aspect('equal')
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    
    # Print mathematical relationships
    print("=== Decision Boundary Mathematics ===")
    print("General form: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0")
    print("Line form: x₂ = -(w₁/w₂)x₁ - (b/w₂)")
    print("Slope = -w₁/w₂")
    print("y-intercept = -b/w₂")
    print("Weight vector [w₁, w₂] is perpendicular to the boundary")
    print("Distance from origin = |b|/√(w₁² + w₂²)")

# Create the decision boundary visualization
draw_decision_boundary_concept()

=== Decision Boundary Mathematics ===
General form: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0
Line form: x₂ = -(w₁/w₂)x₁ - (b/w₂)
Slope = -w₁/w₂
y-intercept = -b/w₂
Weight vector [w₁, w₂] is perpendicular to the boundary
Distance from origin = |b|/√(w₁² + w₂²)

Gradient-Based Learning¶

The neuron learns by adjusting weights and bias using gradient descent to minimize the loss function.

Mathematical Notation Clarification¶

Important distinction:

  • $z = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b$ (linear combination, pre-activation)
  • $y = f(z) = \sigma(z)$ (output after activation function)

Loss Functions¶

For Binary Classification (with sigmoid activation):

Binary Cross-Entropy Loss with true label $t \in \{0, 1\}$ and prediction $y$:

$$L_{BCE} = -[t \log y + (1-t) \log(1-y)]$$

For Regression (with linear activation):

Mean Square Error Loss with true value $t$ and prediction $y$:

$$L_{MSE} = \frac{1}{2}(y - t)^2$$

Gradients for Both Loss Functions¶

Using chain rule: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w_i}$

For MSE Loss (regression with linear activation $y = z$):

$$\frac{\partial L_{MSE}}{\partial w_i} = (y - t) \cdot x_i$$

$$\frac{\partial L_{MSE}}{\partial b} = (y - t)$$

For BCE Loss (classification with sigmoid activation $y = \sigma(z)$):

The BCE gradients are more complex before simplification:

$$\frac{\partial L_{BCE}}{\partial w_i} = \left[\frac{y - t}{y(1-y)}\right] \cdot y(1-y) \cdot x_i = (y - t) \cdot x_i$$

$$\frac{\partial L_{BCE}}{\partial b} = (y - t)$$

Remarkable coincidence: Both MSE and BCE with sigmoid give the same gradient form!

  • MSE: Direct derivative of $\frac{1}{2}(y-t)^2$
  • BCE + Sigmoid: The sigmoid derivative $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$ perfectly cancels with BCE's derivative, yielding the same simple form

Parameter Updates¶

Using learning rate $\eta$:

$$w_i \leftarrow w_i - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i}$$

$$b \leftarrow b - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$$

The decision boundary rotates and translates during training to better separate the classes.

In [29]:
# Demonstrate the gradient calculation for both MSE and BCE
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import numpy as np

print("=== Gradient Calculation Demonstration ===\n")

# Sample data
x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=False)
t_reg = torch.tensor([3.5])  # Regression target
t_cls = torch.tensor([1.0])  # Classification target

# Parameters (with gradient tracking)
w = torch.tensor([1.5], requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor([0.5], requires_grad=True)

print("Sample input x =", x.item())
print("Regression target t =", t_reg.item())
print("Classification target t =", t_cls.item())
print("Initial weight w =", w.item())
print("Initial bias b =", b.item())

# === MSE Case (Regression) ===
print("\n🔢 MSE LOSS (Regression):")

# Forward pass (linear activation)
z_reg = w * x + b
y_reg = z_reg  # Linear activation: y = z
mse_loss = 0.5 * (y_reg - t_reg)**2

print(f"z = wx + b = {w.item():.2f} × {x.item():.2f} + {b.item():.2f} = {z_reg.item():.2f}")
print(f"y = z = {y_reg.item():.2f} (linear activation)")
print(f"MSE Loss = 0.5 × (y - t)² = 0.5 × ({y_reg.item():.2f} - {t_reg.item():.2f})² = {mse_loss.item():.4f}")

# Compute gradients
mse_loss.backward()
print(f"∂L/∂w = (y - t) × x = ({y_reg.item():.2f} - {t_reg.item():.2f}) × {x.item():.2f} = {w.grad.item():.2f}")
print(f"∂L/∂b = (y - t) = ({y_reg.item():.2f} - {t_reg.item():.2f}) = {b.grad.item():.2f}")

# Reset gradients
w.grad.zero_()
b.grad.zero_()

# === BCE Case (Classification) ===
print("\n🎯 BCE LOSS (Classification):")

# Forward pass (sigmoid activation)
z_cls = w * x + b
y_cls = torch.sigmoid(z_cls)  # Sigmoid activation
bce_loss = -(t_cls * torch.log(y_cls) + (1 - t_cls) * torch.log(1 - y_cls))

print(f"z = wx + b = {w.item():.2f} × {x.item():.2f} + {b.item():.2f} = {z_cls.item():.2f}")
print(f"y = σ(z) = σ({z_cls.item():.2f}) = {y_cls.item():.4f} (sigmoid activation)")
print(f"BCE Loss = -[t×log(y) + (1-t)×log(1-y)] = {bce_loss.item():.4f}")

# Compute gradients
bce_loss.backward()
print(f"∂L/∂w = (y - t) × x = ({y_cls.item():.4f} - {t_cls.item():.2f}) × {x.item():.2f} = {w.grad.item():.4f}")
print(f"∂L/∂b = (y - t) = ({y_cls.item():.4f} - {t_cls.item():.2f}) = {b.grad.item():.4f}")

# === Mathematical Explanation ===
print("\n📚 MATHEMATICAL BREAKDOWN:")
print("\nFor MSE (y = z, linear activation):")
print("L = ½(y - t)²")
print("∂L/∂y = (y - t)")
print("∂y/∂z = 1  (linear activation)")
print("∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂y × ∂y/∂z × ∂z/∂w = (y - t) × 1 × x = (y - t) × x")

print("\nFor BCE (y = σ(z), sigmoid activation):")
print("L = -[t×log(y) + (1-t)×log(1-y)]")
print("∂L/∂y = -(t/y - (1-t)/(1-y)) = (y - t)/(y(1-y))")
print("∂y/∂z = σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)) = y(1-y)  (sigmoid derivative)")
print("∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂y × ∂y/∂z × ∂z/∂w = [(y-t)/(y(1-y))] × [y(1-y)] × x = (y - t) × x")

print("\n🎉 REMARKABLE RESULT:")
print("Both MSE and BCE+sigmoid give the SAME gradient formula: (y - t) × x")
print("This is why the gradient descent update looks identical for both cases!")

# Demonstrate the cancellation visually
print(f"\nNumerical verification:")
y_val = y_cls.item()
t_val = t_cls.item()
x_val = x.item()

# BCE gradient breakdown
bce_dy = (y_val - t_val) / (y_val * (1 - y_val))  # ∂L/∂y for BCE  
sigmoid_dz = y_val * (1 - y_val)                  # ∂y/∂z for sigmoid
dz_dw = x_val                                     # ∂z/∂w

print(f"BCE: ∂L/∂y = (y-t)/(y(1-y)) = {bce_dy:.4f}")
print(f"Sigmoid: ∂y/∂z = y(1-y) = {sigmoid_dz:.4f}")
print(f"Chain rule: ∂L/∂w = {bce_dy:.4f} × {sigmoid_dz:.4f} × {dz_dw:.1f} = {bce_dy * sigmoid_dz * dz_dw:.4f}")
print(f"Direct: (y - t) × x = ({y_val:.4f} - {t_val:.1f}) × {x_val:.1f} = {(y_val - t_val) * x_val:.4f}")
print("✅ They match! The y(1-y) terms cancel perfectly.")

=== Gradient Calculation Demonstration ===

Sample input x = 2.0
Regression target t = 3.5
Classification target t = 1.0
Initial weight w = 1.5
Initial bias b = 0.5

🔢 MSE LOSS (Regression):
z = wx + b = 1.50 × 2.00 + 0.50 = 3.50
y = z = 3.50 (linear activation)
MSE Loss = 0.5 × (y - t)² = 0.5 × (3.50 - 3.50)² = 0.0000
∂L/∂w = (y - t) × x = (3.50 - 3.50) × 2.00 = 0.00
∂L/∂b = (y - t) = (3.50 - 3.50) = 0.00

🎯 BCE LOSS (Classification):
z = wx + b = 1.50 × 2.00 + 0.50 = 3.50
y = σ(z) = σ(3.50) = 0.9707 (sigmoid activation)
BCE Loss = -[t×log(y) + (1-t)×log(1-y)] = 0.0298
∂L/∂w = (y - t) × x = (0.9707 - 1.00) × 2.00 = -0.0586
∂L/∂b = (y - t) = (0.9707 - 1.00) = -0.0293

📚 MATHEMATICAL BREAKDOWN:

For MSE (y = z, linear activation):
L = ½(y - t)²
∂L/∂y = (y - t)
∂y/∂z = 1  (linear activation)
∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂y × ∂y/∂z × ∂z/∂w = (y - t) × 1 × x = (y - t) × x

For BCE (y = σ(z), sigmoid activation):
L = -[t×log(y) + (1-t)×log(1-y)]
∂L/∂y = -(t/y - (1-t)/(1-y)) = (y - t)/(y(1-y))
∂y/∂z = σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)) = y(1-y)  (sigmoid derivative)
∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂y × ∂y/∂z × ∂z/∂w = [(y-t)/(y(1-y))] × [y(1-y)] × x = (y - t) × x

🎉 REMARKABLE RESULT:
Both MSE and BCE+sigmoid give the SAME gradient formula: (y - t) × x
This is why the gradient descent update looks identical for both cases!

Numerical verification:
BCE: ∂L/∂y = (y-t)/(y(1-y)) = -1.0302
Sigmoid: ∂y/∂z = y(1-y) = 0.0285
Chain rule: ∂L/∂w = -1.0302 × 0.0285 × 2.0 = -0.0586
Direct: (y - t) × x = (0.9707 - 1.0) × 2.0 = -0.0586
✅ They match! The y(1-y) terms cancel perfectly.

Gradient Descent Algorithm Philosophy¶

The fundamental principle of gradient descent is to iteratively move in the direction opposite to the gradient to find the minimum of a loss function. This process can be visualized as a ball rolling down a hill, where:

  • The hill represents the loss landscape
  • The ball's position represents current parameter values
  • The slope at any point is the gradient
  • Rolling downhill means moving opposite to the gradient direction

Mathematical Foundation¶

Given a loss function $L(\mathbf{w}, b)$ where $\mathbf{w}$ are weights and $b$ is bias:

  1. Compute gradient: $\nabla L = \left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\right]^T$

  2. Update parameters: $\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$

  3. Repeat until convergence: Continue until $|\nabla L| < \epsilon$ or maximum iterations reached

Key Concepts¶

  • Learning rate $\eta$: Controls step size (too large → overshoot, too small → slow convergence)
  • Local minima: Algorithm finds nearby minimum, not necessarily global minimum
  • Convergence: Process stops when gradient approaches zero
  • Trajectory: Path taken through parameter space during optimization
In [23]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D
import matplotlib.patches as patches

def create_loss_surface():
    """Create a complex 2D loss function for visualization."""
    x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
    y = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
    
    # Complex loss surface with multiple local minima
    Z = (X**2 + Y**2 - 2*X - 2*Y + 2 + 
         0.3*np.sin(3*X) + 0.3*np.cos(3*Y) + 
         0.1*(X-1)**4 + 0.1*(Y-1)**4)
    
    return X, Y, Z

def gradient_2d(x, y):
    """Compute gradient of the loss function at point (x, y)."""
    # Analytical gradient of our loss function
    dx = 2*x - 2 + 0.9*np.cos(3*x) + 0.4*(x-1)**3
    dy = 2*y - 2 - 0.9*np.sin(3*y) + 0.4*(y-1)**3
    return dx, dy

def gradient_descent_trajectory(start_x, start_y, learning_rate=0.1, max_iter=50):
    """Simulate gradient descent trajectory."""
    trajectory = [(start_x, start_y)]
    x, y = start_x, start_y
    
    for i in range(max_iter):
        # Compute gradient
        dx, dy = gradient_2d(x, y)
        
        # Update parameters (move opposite to gradient)
        x = x - learning_rate * dx
        y = y - learning_rate * dy
        
        trajectory.append((x, y))
        
        # Stop if gradient is very small (convergence)
        if np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2) < 0.01:
            break
    
    return np.array(trajectory)

# Create comprehensive gradient descent visualization
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(18, 12))

# === Plot 1: 3D Loss Surface with Trajectory ===
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 1, projection='3d')
X, Y, Z = create_loss_surface()

# Plot surface
surf = ax1.plot_surface(X, Y, Z, cmap='viridis', alpha=0.6, linewidth=0, antialiased=True)

# Add gradient descent trajectory
start_point = (-2, 2)
trajectory = gradient_descent_trajectory(start_point[0], start_point[1], learning_rate=0.1)

# Compute loss values along trajectory
traj_z = []
for tx, ty in trajectory:
    tz = (tx**2 + ty**2 - 2*tx - 2*ty + 2 + 
          0.3*np.sin(3*tx) + 0.3*np.cos(3*ty) + 
          0.1*(tx-1)**4 + 0.1*(ty-1)**4)
    traj_z.append(tz)

# Plot trajectory
ax1.plot(trajectory[:, 0], trajectory[:, 1], traj_z, 'r-', linewidth=3, label='Gradient Descent Path')
ax1.plot([trajectory[0, 0]], [trajectory[0, 1]], [traj_z[0]], 'go', markersize=10, label='Start')
ax1.plot([trajectory[-1, 0]], [trajectory[-1, 1]], [traj_z[-1]], 'ro', markersize=10, label='End')

ax1.set_title('3D Loss Surface with Gradient Descent', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax1.set_xlabel('Weight w₁')
ax1.set_ylabel('Weight w₂')
ax1.set_zlabel('Loss L(w₁, w₂)')
ax1.legend()

# === Plot 2: 2D Contour with Trajectory ===
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 2)
contour = ax2.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=20, colors='gray', alpha=0.6)
ax2.contourf(X, Y, Z, levels=20, cmap='viridis', alpha=0.3)

# Plot trajectory
ax2.plot(trajectory[:, 0], trajectory[:, 1], 'r-', linewidth=3, label='Optimization Path')
ax2.plot(trajectory[0, 0], trajectory[0, 1], 'go', markersize=10, label='Start Point')
ax2.plot(trajectory[-1, 0], trajectory[-1, 1], 'ro', markersize=10, label='Converged Point')

# Add gradient arrows at several points
for i in range(0, len(trajectory)-1, 5):
    x, y = trajectory[i]
    dx, dy = gradient_2d(x, y)
    # Normalize for visualization
    norm = np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2)
    if norm > 0:
        dx, dy = dx/norm * 0.3, dy/norm * 0.3
        # Gradient arrow (pointing uphill)
        ax2.arrow(x, y, dx, dy, head_width=0.08, head_length=0.08, 
                 fc='blue', ec='blue', alpha=0.7, linewidth=1.5)
        # Step arrow (pointing downhill, opposite to gradient)
        ax2.arrow(x, y, -dx, -dy, head_width=0.08, head_length=0.08, 
                 fc='orange', ec='orange', alpha=0.8, linewidth=2)

ax2.set_title('Contour View: Following Negative Gradient', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax2.set_xlabel('Weight w₁')
ax2.set_ylabel('Weight w₂')
ax2.legend()
ax2.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax2.set_aspect('equal')

# === Plot 3: Loss vs Iteration ===
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 3)
iterations = range(len(traj_z))
ax3.plot(iterations, traj_z, 'b-', linewidth=2, marker='o', markersize=4)
ax3.set_title('Loss Decrease Over Iterations', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax3.set_xlabel('Iteration')
ax3.set_ylabel('Loss Value')
ax3.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Annotate key points
ax3.annotate(f'Start: L={traj_z[0]:.2f}', xy=(0, traj_z[0]), xytext=(5, traj_z[0]+0.5),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='green'), fontsize=10)
ax3.annotate(f'End: L={traj_z[-1]:.2f}', xy=(len(traj_z)-1, traj_z[-1]), 
            xytext=(len(traj_z)-10, traj_z[-1]+0.5),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red'), fontsize=10)

# === Plot 4: Different Learning Rates Comparison ===
ax4 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 4)
learning_rates = [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2]
colors = ['blue', 'green', 'red', 'orange']

for lr, color in zip(learning_rates, colors):
    traj = gradient_descent_trajectory(-2, 2, learning_rate=lr, max_iter=100)
    ax4.plot(traj[:, 0], traj[:, 1], color=color, linewidth=2, 
            label=f'η = {lr}', alpha=0.8)
    ax4.plot(traj[0, 0], traj[0, 1], 'o', color=color, markersize=8)
    ax4.plot(traj[-1, 0], traj[-1, 1], 's', color=color, markersize=8)

# Add contour background
ax4.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=15, colors='gray', alpha=0.4)
ax4.set_title('Effect of Learning Rate on Convergence', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax4.set_xlabel('Weight w₁')
ax4.set_ylabel('Weight w₂')
ax4.legend()
ax4.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax4.set_aspect('equal')

# === Plot 5: Gradient Vector Field ===
ax5 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 5)
# Create a coarser grid for vector field
x_vec = np.linspace(-3, 3, 15)
y_vec = np.linspace(-3, 3, 15)
X_vec, Y_vec = np.meshgrid(x_vec, y_vec)

# Compute gradients at each point
DX = np.zeros_like(X_vec)
DY = np.zeros_like(Y_vec)
for i in range(X_vec.shape[0]):
    for j in range(X_vec.shape[1]):
        dx, dy = gradient_2d(X_vec[i, j], Y_vec[i, j])
        DX[i, j] = dx
        DY[i, j] = dy

# Normalize vectors for better visualization
norm = np.sqrt(DX**2 + DY**2)
DX_norm = DX / (norm + 1e-8)
DY_norm = DY / (norm + 1e-8)

# Plot vector field (gradient directions)
ax5.quiver(X_vec, Y_vec, DX_norm, DY_norm, norm, cmap='plasma', alpha=0.7, scale=20)
ax5.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=15, colors='black', alpha=0.3)

# Add sample trajectory
sample_traj = gradient_descent_trajectory(-1.5, 1.5, learning_rate=0.08)
ax5.plot(sample_traj[:, 0], sample_traj[:, 1], 'white', linewidth=3, alpha=0.9)
ax5.plot(sample_traj[0, 0], sample_traj[0, 1], 'go', markersize=10)
ax5.plot(sample_traj[-1, 0], sample_traj[-1, 1], 'ro', markersize=10)

ax5.set_title('Gradient Vector Field & Optimization Path', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax5.set_xlabel('Weight w₁')
ax5.set_ylabel('Weight w₂')
ax5.set_aspect('equal')

# === Plot 6: Algorithm Conceptual Diagram ===
ax6 = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, 6)
ax6.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax6.set_ylim(0, 8)

# Draw algorithm flowchart
# Start
start_box = patches.FancyBboxPatch((0.5, 6.5), 2, 1, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", 
                                  facecolor='lightgreen', edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
ax6.add_patch(start_box)
ax6.text(1.5, 7, 'Initialize\nParameters', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# Compute gradient
grad_box = patches.FancyBboxPatch((0.5, 4.5), 2, 1, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", 
                                 facecolor='lightblue', edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
ax6.add_patch(grad_box)
ax6.text(1.5, 5, 'Compute\nGradient ∇L', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# Update parameters
update_box = patches.FancyBboxPatch((0.5, 2.5), 2, 1, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", 
                                   facecolor='lightyellow', edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
ax6.add_patch(update_box)
ax6.text(1.5, 3, 'Update:\nw ← w - η∇L', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# Decision diamond
decision_points = np.array([[4, 4], [5.5, 5], [7, 4], [5.5, 3]])
decision = patches.Polygon(decision_points, facecolor='lightcoral', edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
ax6.add_patch(decision)
ax6.text(5.5, 4, 'Converged?', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# End
end_box = patches.FancyBboxPatch((7.5, 6.5), 2, 1, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", 
                                facecolor='lightcoral', edgecolor='black', linewidth=2)
ax6.add_patch(end_box)
ax6.text(8.5, 7, 'Optimal\nParameters', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold')

# Arrows
arrows = [
    ((1.5, 6.5), (1.5, 5.5)),  # Start to gradient
    ((1.5, 4.5), (1.5, 3.5)),  # Gradient to update
    ((2.5, 3), (4, 4)),        # Update to decision
    ((7, 4), (7.5, 7)),        # Decision to end (Yes)
    ((5.5, 3), (1.5, 2.5)),    # Decision to update (No) - loop back
]

for start, end in arrows:
    ax6.annotate('', xy=end, xytext=start, 
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=2, color='black'))

# Labels for decision paths
ax6.text(7.2, 5.5, 'Yes', fontweight='bold', color='green', fontsize=12)
ax6.text(3, 2.2, 'No', fontweight='bold', color='red', fontsize=12)

# Mathematical annotations
ax6.text(5, 0.5, r'$\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla L(\mathbf{w}^{(t)})$', 
         fontsize=14, ha='center', bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", facecolor='white', alpha=0.8))

ax6.set_title('Gradient Descent Algorithm Flow', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
ax6.axis('off')

Algorithm Flowchart¶

\begin{tikzpicture}[
    node distance=1.5cm,
    start/.style={ellipse, draw, fill=green!20, minimum width=2.5cm, minimum height=1cm},
    process/.style={rectangle, draw, fill=blue!20, minimum width=2.5cm, minimum height=1cm, rounded corners},

    % Nodes
    \node[start] (init) {Initialize\\$\mathbf{w}^{(0)}, b^{(0)}$};
    \node[process, below of=init] (forward) {Forward Pass\\$y = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b)$};
    \node[process, below of=forward] (loss) {Compute Loss\\$L = -[t\log y + (1-t)\log(1-y)]$};
    \node[process, below of=loss] (gradient) {Compute Gradient\\$\nabla L = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{w}}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$};
    \node[process, below of=gradient] (update) {Update Parameters\\$\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}L$\\$b \leftarrow b - \eta\nabla_b L$};
    \node[decision, below of=update] (converged) {Converged?\\$|\nabla L| < \epsilon$};
    \node[end, below of=converged] (finish) {Optimal\\Parameters};
    
    % Arrows
    \draw[arrow] (init) -- (forward);
    \draw[arrow] (forward) -- (loss);
    \draw[arrow] (loss) -- (gradient);
    \draw[arrow] (gradient) -- (update);
    \draw[arrow] (update) -- (converged);
    \draw[arrow] (converged) -- (finish) node[midway, right] {Yes};
    
    % Loop back arrow
    \draw[arrow] (converged.west) -- ++(-2,0) -- ++(0,4) -- (forward.west) node[midway, left] {No};
    
    % Mathematical insight box
    \node at (6, -2) [draw, fill=white, align=left, font=\footnotesize] {
        \textbf{Key Insight:}\\
        Follow negative gradient\\
        $\nabla L$ points uphill\\
        $-\nabla L$ points downhill\\
        Step size controlled by $\eta$
    };

\end{tikzpicture}

Key TikZ Components:

  • 3D surface representation: Shows the loss landscape as a hill
  • Trajectory visualization: Red path showing parameter updates
  • Gradient vectors: Blue arrows pointing uphill (gradient direction)
  • Step vectors: Orange arrows pointing downhill (update direction)
  • Flowchart elements: Algorithm structure with decision points
  • Mathematical annotations: Key equations and relationships

Key Insights from Gradient Descent Visualization¶

The comprehensive visualizations above demonstrate several critical concepts:

1. Ball Rolling Downhill Analogy¶

  • The loss function creates a "landscape" where higher values represent hills
  • The algorithm is like a ball that always rolls downhill (negative gradient direction)
  • The gradient $\nabla L$ points uphill (steepest increase)
  • We move opposite to gradient: $-\nabla L$ (steepest decrease)

2. Iterative Optimization Process¶

  • Start: Initialize parameters at some random point in parameter space
  • Repeat: Compute gradient → Take step opposite to gradient → Update parameters
  • Stop: When gradient becomes very small (near flat region = minimum)

3. Learning Rate Critical Role¶

  • Too small ($\eta \ll 1$): Slow convergence, many iterations needed
  • Optimal ($\eta$ moderate): Fast, stable convergence to minimum
  • Too large ($\eta \gg 1$): Oscillations, possible divergence, overshooting

4. Geometric Interpretation¶

  • Contour lines: Represent equal loss values (like elevation lines on a map)
  • Gradient vectors: Always perpendicular to contour lines, point "uphill"
  • Optimization path: Zigzag pattern following steepest descent at each point
  • Convergence: Path spirals into the minimum point

5. Local vs Global Optimization¶

  • Gradient descent finds local minima, not necessarily global minimum
  • Starting point affects which minimum is found
  • Complex loss landscapes have multiple local minima
  • Neural networks often have many local minima, but most are "good enough"

Mathematical Guarantees¶

For convex functions (single bowl-shaped minimum):

  • Gradient descent always converges to global minimum
  • Convergence rate depends on condition number of the loss function
  • Linear neurons create convex loss landscapes for appropriate loss functions

For non-convex functions (neural networks):

  • Convergence to local minimum
  • No guarantee of global optimum
  • Empirically works well for deep learning

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

# Set random seeds for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

class ClassificationNeuron(nn.Module):
    """Single neuron for binary classification with decision boundary analysis."""
    
    def __init__(self):
        super(ClassificationNeuron, self).__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(2, 1)  # 2D input -> 1 output
        
        # Initialize with small random weights
        nn.init.normal_(self.linear.weight, 0, 0.1)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.linear.bias)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.linear(x)
        return torch.sigmoid(z)
    
    def get_decision_boundary(self, x_range=(-3, 3)):
        """
        Get decision boundary line points.
        Decision boundary: w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b = 0
        Rearranged: x2 = -(w1/w2)*x1 - (b/w2)
        """
        w1, w2 = self.linear.weight.data[0]
        b = self.linear.bias.data[0]
        
        x1_points = np.linspace(x_range[0], x_range[1], 100)
        
        # Avoid division by zero
        if abs(w2) < 1e-6:
            # Vertical line: x1 = -b/w1
            x1_line = -b/w1 if abs(w1) > 1e-6 else 0
            return np.full_like(x1_points, x1_line), x1_points
        else:
            x2_points = -(w1/w2) * x1_points - (b/w2)
            return x1_points, x2_points

# Generate linearly separable 2D dataset
print("=== Decision Boundary Learning Demo ===")
X_np, y_np = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=2, n_redundant=0, 
                                n_informative=2, n_clusters_per_class=1, 
                                class_sep=1.5, random_state=42)

# Convert to PyTorch tensors
X = torch.FloatTensor(X_np)
y = torch.FloatTensor(y_np).unsqueeze(1)

print(f"Dataset shape: {X.shape}")
print(f"Class distribution: {torch.bincount(y.squeeze().long())}")

# Create and train the neuron
neuron = ClassificationNeuron()
criterion = nn.BCELoss()
optimizer = optim.SGD(neuron.parameters(), lr=0.1)

# Training parameters
epochs = [0, 5, 20, 100]  # Epochs at which to visualize
losses = []
boundary_evolution = []

# Store initial state
w_init = neuron.linear.weight.data.clone()
b_init = neuron.linear.bias.data.clone()
boundary_evolution.append((w_init.clone(), b_init.clone()))

print(f"\nInitial parameters:")
print(f"Weights: [{w_init[0,0]:.3f}, {w_init[0,1]:.3f}]")
print(f"Bias: {b_init[0]:.3f}")

# Training loop with visualization
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 12))
axes = axes.flatten()

epoch_idx = 0
current_epoch = 0

for epoch in range(max(epochs) + 1):
    # Forward pass
    outputs = neuron(X)
    loss = criterion(outputs, y)
    
    # Backward pass
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    
    losses.append(loss.item())
    
    # Store parameters at key epochs
    if epoch in epochs:
        w_current = neuron.linear.weight.data.clone()
        b_current = neuron.linear.bias.data.clone()
        boundary_evolution.append((w_current.clone(), b_current.clone()))
        
        # Plot current state
        ax = axes[epoch_idx]
        
        # Plot data points
        colors = ['red' if label == 0 else 'blue' for label in y_np]
        ax.scatter(X_np[:, 0], X_np[:, 1], c=colors, alpha=0.7, s=50)
        
        # Plot decision boundary
        w1, w2 = w_current[0]
        b = b_current[0]
        
        # Create decision boundary line
        try:
            if abs(w2) > 1e-6:  # Non-vertical line
                x1_boundary = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
                x2_boundary = -(w1/w2) * x1_boundary - (b/w2)
                
                # Plot the decision boundary line
                ax.plot(x1_boundary, x2_boundary, 'black', linewidth=2, 
                       label='Decision Boundary', linestyle='-')
            else:  # Vertical line
                if abs(w1) > 1e-6:
                    x1_boundary_val = -b/w1
                    ax.axvline(x=x1_boundary_val, color='black', linewidth=2, 
                             label='Decision Boundary', linestyle='-')
        except Exception as e:
            # Fallback: draw a simple line through the center
            x1_center = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
            if abs(w2) > 1e-6:
                x2_center = -(w1/w2) * x1_center - (b/w2)
                ax.plot(x1_center, x2_center, 'black', linewidth=2, 
                       label='Decision Boundary', linestyle='-', alpha=0.7)
        
        # Add background coloring for regions
        x1_mesh, x2_mesh = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 50), np.linspace(-3, 3, 50))
        z_mesh = w1 * x1_mesh + w2 * x2_mesh + b
        ax.contourf(x1_mesh, x2_mesh, z_mesh, levels=[-1000, 0, 1000], 
                   colors=['lightcoral', 'lightblue'], alpha=0.2)
        
        # Calculate accuracy
        with torch.no_grad():
            predictions = (outputs > 0.5).float()
            accuracy = (predictions == y).float().mean()
        
        # Format title with parameters
        w1, w2 = w_current[0]
        b = b_current[0]
        ax.set_title(f'Epoch {epoch} (Acc: {accuracy:.1%})\n'
                    f'w=[{w1:.2f}, {w2:.2f}], b={b:.2f}\n'
                    f'Boundary: {w2:.2f}x₂ = -{w1:.2f}x₁ - {b:.2f}')
        
        ax.set_xlabel('x₁')
        ax.set_ylabel('x₂')
        ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
        ax.set_xlim(-3, 3)
        ax.set_ylim(-3, 3)
        ax.legend()
        
        epoch_idx += 1

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Final analysis
print(f"\n=== Decision Boundary Evolution Analysis ===")
final_w = neuron.linear.weight.data[0]
final_b = neuron.linear.bias.data[0]

print(f"Final parameters:")
print(f"Weights: [{final_w[0]:.3f}, {final_w[1]:.3f}]")
print(f"Bias: {final_b:.3f}")

# Final accuracy
with torch.no_grad():
    final_outputs = neuron(X)
    final_predictions = (final_outputs > 0.5).float()
    final_accuracy = (final_predictions == y).float().mean()
    print(f"Final accuracy: {final_accuracy:.1%}")

# Decision boundary analysis
print(f"\nDecision boundary equation: {final_w[0]:.3f}x₁ + {final_w[1]:.3f}x₂ + {final_b:.3f} = 0")
if abs(final_w[1]) > 1e-6:
    slope = -final_w[0] / final_w[1]
    intercept = -final_b / final_w[1]
    print(f"Line form: x₂ = {slope:.3f}x₁ + {intercept:.3f}")

# Weight vector interpretation
weight_magnitude = torch.norm(final_w)
weight_direction = final_w / weight_magnitude
print(f"\nWeight vector magnitude: {weight_magnitude:.3f}")
print(f"Weight vector direction (unit): [{weight_direction[0]:.3f}, {weight_direction[1]:.3f}]")
print(f"Weight vector angle: {torch.atan2(weight_direction[1], weight_direction[0]) * 180 / np.pi:.1f}°")

# Distance from origin to decision boundary
distance_to_origin = abs(final_b) / weight_magnitude
print(f"Distance from origin to boundary: {distance_to_origin:.3f}")

# Plot training loss
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(losses)
plt.title('Training Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy)')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.grid(True)

# Plot gradient magnitude over training
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
# Compute gradient magnitudes manually for demonstration
gradient_mags = []
for i in range(0, len(losses), 10):  # Sample every 10 epochs
    # Reset to state at epoch i and compute gradients
    with torch.no_grad():
        # Approximate gradient magnitude from loss change
        if i > 0:
            grad_approx = abs(losses[i] - losses[i-1]) * 10  # Scaled for visibility
            gradient_mags.append(grad_approx)

plt.plot(range(0, len(losses), 10)[:len(gradient_mags)], gradient_mags)
plt.title('Approximate Gradient Magnitude')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.ylabel('Gradient Magnitude')
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"\n=== Generalization to Higher Dimensions ===")
print("In 2D: Decision boundary is a LINE")
print("In 3D: Decision boundary is a PLANE") 
print("In nD: Decision boundary is a HYPERPLANE")
print("Formula: w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + wₙxₙ + b = 0")
print("\nThis single neuron concept generalizes to:")
print("• Multi-class: Multiple hyperplanes (one-vs-rest)")
print("• Non-linear: Multiple neurons create CONVEX HULLS") 
print("• Deep networks: Combinations of convex regions")

Generalization to Higher Dimensions¶

The 2D decision boundary concept is fundamental to understanding neural networks in higher dimensions:

Linear Separability¶

A single neuron can only learn linearly separable patterns:

  • 2D: Points separated by a line
  • 3D: Points separated by a plane
  • nD: Points separated by a hyperplane

The hyperplane equation in $n$-dimensional space: $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b = 0$$

Geometric Properties¶

  1. Normal vector: $\mathbf{w} = [w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n]^T$ is perpendicular to the hyperplane
  2. Distance to origin: $\frac{|b|}{||\mathbf{w}||}$
  3. Classification: Based on which side of hyperplane points fall

Limitations and Extensions¶

Single Neuron Limitations:

  • Can only create one hyperplane
  • Cannot solve XOR problem (non-linearly separable)
  • Limited to convex decision regions

Multi-Neuron Extensions:

  • Multiple neurons → Multiple hyperplanes → Convex hull regions
  • Hidden layers → Combinations of convex regions → Complex boundaries
  • Deep networks → Arbitrary decision boundaries

This progression from line → hyperplane → convex hull → complex regions is the mathematical foundation of how neural networks increase in representational power.

Summary¶

The artificial neuron is a fundamental component that:

Core Functionality¶

  1. Receives multiple inputs $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$
  2. Weights each input with learnable parameters $(w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n)$
  3. Adds a bias term $b$
  4. Applies an activation function $f$
  5. Produces a single output $y$

Decision Boundary Capability¶

  • Creates linear decision boundaries (hyperplanes) in input space
  • Separates binary classes using the equation $\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} + b = 0$
  • Learns through gradient descent by rotating and translating the boundary
  • Generalizes from 2D lines to higher-dimensional hyperplanes

Mathematical Foundation¶

  • Linear separability: Can only solve linearly separable problems
  • Geometric interpretation: Weight vector is perpendicular to decision boundary
  • Learning dynamics: Gradients adjust parameters to minimize classification error
  • Scaling pathway: Single neuron → multiple neurons → convex hulls → complex boundaries

Key Properties¶

  • Learnable parameters: Weights and bias adjusted during training
  • Differentiable: Enables gradient-based optimization
  • Geometrically interpretable: Clear relationship between parameters and decision boundary
  • Fundamental building block: Basis for multilayer perceptrons, CNNs, and transformers

This component serves as the mathematical and conceptual foundation for understanding how neural networks learn to partition input spaces and make predictions.

Next Steps in Neural Network Components¶

Building on the Foundation¶

The artificial neuron is the fundamental building block, but neural networks become powerful through:

  1. Multiple Neurons: Combining many neurons in layers
  2. Deep Architectures: Stacking layers to create complex functions
  3. Specialized Components: Different types of layers and connections

Key Components to Explore¶

  • Activation Functions: Deep dive into the non-linear transformations that make learning possible
  • Layer Types: Dense/Linear, Convolutional, Recurrent layers
  • Optimization: How networks learn through backpropagation and gradient descent
  • Regularization: Techniques to prevent overfitting and improve generalization

From Single Neuron to Deep Networks¶

Single Neuron → Multi-layer Perceptron → Deep Neural Networks → Specialized Architectures
     ↓                    ↓                        ↓                       ↓
Linear Separation    Non-linear Boundaries    Universal Approximation    Task-specific Solutions

The journey from understanding a single neuron to mastering deep learning involves progressively building complexity while maintaining mathematical rigor and practical understanding.
